post.description:
Register a new agent and issue a device certificate.

Validates the enrollment token when ``SENTARI_ENROLLMENT_TOKEN`` is set.
Issues a real mTLS client certificate signed by the internal CA.
Rate-limited to 10 registrations per IP per minute.

Re-issue a device certificate over the authenticated mTLS channel.

Unlike ``/register``, renewal carries **no enrollment token** — the
current, still-valid mTLS cert *is* the authentication
(``verify_agent_cert`` + ``require_cert_role``).  Identity is taken from
the cert-resolved device, never from the request body: the same
``device_id`` and ``role`` are preserved and the re-issued cert uses the
device's stored hostname (the CSR subject is discarded by ``sign_csr``).

To survive a lost renew response (the res-007 strand gap), the superseded
fingerprint is kept in ``certificate_fingerprint_previous`` and stays
accepted by ``verify_agent_cert`` until ``certificate_previous_not_after``
(``now + _RENEW_OVERLAP_WINDOW``): a device that didn't receive the new
cert keeps working on its old one and simply retries next cycle.  The
write runs under ``SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`` on the device row so concurrent
renews serialise — the loser's cert lands in the previous slot rather than
being lost.

Receive scan results from an agent (mTLS required in production).

Validates the device_id, stores the scan and individual package records in
TimescaleDB, and writes an audit log entry. Then enqueues the
``correlate_scan`` Celery task for asynchronous CVE correlation.

Re-anchor an agent's local audit-log entries server-side.

The agent's on-device hash chain is only tamper-*evident* once an
independent party witnesses it. The server re-verifies each shipped
entry's hash and its linkage (within the batch and against previously
witnessed entries for the device), stores them as append-only forensic
records, and on any divergence raises an integrity alert plus a
server-side audit_log entry. Always returns 202 (even on a detected
violation — the failure is reported in the body and alerted, not
rejected, so the evidence is preserved).

get.description:
Return the current agent configuration (mTLS required in production).

Agents poll this endpoint at their configured interval.
Future: reads from system_config table for per-device overrides.

Return a signed envelope containing the current SPDX + tier mapping.

The envelope has the shape ``{payload, signature, key_id}``; agents
verify the ed25519 signature against a pinned public key before
applying the overlay.  In debug mode, the signing key is auto-generated
on first startup and the public key is logged for developers to pin
into their local agent builds.

Gated by ``verify_agent_cert`` — the license map is not secret, but
the endpoint allocates a non-trivial payload + signature per hit
and we do not want unauthenticated traffic to drive that cost.
A payload that exceeds the 5 MiB envelope cap returns 503 rather
than 500 so agents keep their cached overlay on transient failure.

Also gated on the install-gate master switch (§15a.2): when
disabled, returns 404 + ``X-Sentari-Install-Gate-Disabled: true``
so agents tear down config files immediately.

schema.title: Response Get License Map Api V1 Agent License Map Get

get.description:
Return a signed envelope of vulnerability advisories.

Shape ``{payload, signature, key_id}`` — same as the license-map
envelope.  Agents verify the ed25519 signature against the
``vuln_map_pubkey`` learned at /register time, then apply the
payload to their local vulnerability store for offline
correlation.  In air-gapped deployments this is the only
advisory-delivery channel.

Gated by ``verify_agent_cert`` — the payload can run into tens of
thousands of CVE rows and the DB query behind it is expensive;
exposing it to unauthenticated callers would give anyone who can
reach the API a cheap DoS primitive plus unauthorised access to
the aggregated advisory set.

On fresh installs the signing key is auto-generated on first
access; the paired public key has already been returned on the
agent's most recent /register call (see
``AgentRegisterResponse.vuln_map_pubkey``).  If the key is
unreadable AND auto-generation fails (filesystem permissions),
the endpoint returns 503 — agents treat that as "no update
available" and keep using whatever cached map they already have.
A payload that exceeds the 5 MiB envelope cap also returns 503
(rather than 500) so agents and monitoring treat it as a
transient server-side issue, not a crash.

schema.title: Response Get Vuln Map Api V1 Agent Vuln Map Get

get.description:
Return a signed envelope of active install-gate policies.

Shape: ``{payload, signature, key_id}`` — identical to license-
map and vuln-map.  Agent verifies against the ``install_gate_pubkey``
learned at /register time.  Response includes the proxy endpoints
per ecosystem so a single fetch gives the agent everything it
needs to rewrite native package-manager config files.

When the install-gate master switch is disabled (§15a.2), returns
404 + ``X-Sentari-Install-Gate-Disabled: true`` so agents and
Sentari-Proxy can detect the explicit-disable signal and tear down
any pre-existing config files immediately (rather than waiting for
the 7-day fail-open grace window that applies to plain 404s).

503 on signing-key access failure or payload-size overrun — same
semantics as the other two channels; agent retains the last-good
cached envelope.

schema.title: Response Get Policy Map Api V1 Agent Policy Map Get

get.description:
Return a signed envelope describing the latest agent release.

Shape: ``{payload, signature, key_id}`` — same envelope as
license-map / vuln-map / policy-map.  Agents verify against the
``install_gate_pubkey`` learned at /register and pinned thereafter,
so no new trust anchor is needed for self-update.

Returns 404 when the configured release dir is missing, empty, or
has no binaries matching the manifest's ``latest_version`` — the
agent treats that as "no upgrade available" and keeps polling on
its normal cadence.

Returns 503 only on signing-key access failure (operator error
inside the server) so the agent can distinguish "no update
available right now" (404, keep polling quietly) from "server is
unhealthy" (503, alert).

get.description:
Stream the agent binary for ``(os_name, arch)``.

Path components are validated against the manifest's advertised
platform list — an attacker who can reach this endpoint cannot
coerce path traversal because ``resolve_binary_path`` rejects any
filename containing ``/``, ``\``, or ``..``.  The agent verifies
the SHA256 from the signed manifest after download, so even a
compromised release directory cannot push a forged binary an
enrolled agent will trust.

get.description:
Aggregated runtime versions for a given ecosystem.

Ecosystem-first dashboard contract: PyPI returns the Python
interpreter version distribution (lean ``version`` + ``device_count``
entries — no per-device list, no patch breakdown).  This endpoint
only aggregates the Python interpreter distribution; the other known
ecosystems (npm/maven/nuget/apt/yum) return an empty ``versions``
list here.  (Node/JDK runtime detection ships in the agent and is
surfaced fleet-wide through the runtime-EOL summary + per-device
``/devices/:id/runtimes`` endpoints, not this ecosystem-keyed
aggregation.)  EOL flagging is computed client-side via the
per-ecosystem adapters.  Unknown
ecosystem names return 404 so the dashboard surfaces typos /
stale UI state explicitly.

Per-device install detail is **no longer embedded** here — fetch it on
demand from ``GET /inventory/package-locations``. This
keeps the list payload small and the query a cheap scan of the
``current_installs`` projection instead of a JSON-aggregation over the full
``packages`` history.

post.description:
Authenticate a user and return JWT access + refresh tokens.

For LDAP users the password is validated against the LDAP/AD server.
For local users bcrypt verification is used.
If TOTP is enabled, ``totp_code`` must be provided.

Rate-limited to 5 attempts per IP per 60 seconds.

Exchange a refresh token for a new access token.

Implements RFC 6749 §10.4 refresh-token reuse detection: every
refresh token carries a unique ``jti`` whose row in
``refresh_token_audit`` is flipped from ``used_at IS NULL`` to a
timestamp on first redemption.  A second attempt with the same
jti is an out-of-order replay (the token was stolen or the audit
row was leaked and reused) — the whole token family is then
revoked by bumping ``user.token_generation``, and the caller gets
a 401.

Rate-limited to 5 attempts per IP per 60 seconds.

get.description: Return the authenticated user's profile.

post.description:
Self-service password rotation for the authenticated local user.

Verifies the current password against the stored bcrypt hash via the
same ``verify_password`` helper used at login, enforces the SAME
strength policy as user creation on the new password (in
``PasswordChangeRequest``), and persists a fresh ``hash_password``.

Security choices:

* Federated users (``identity_provider != 'local'``) hit a 400 — they
  have no local password the server controls; their credential lives
  in the upstream IdP.  Mirrors the ``/totp/setup`` re-auth guard.
* A wrong current password returns 401, matching the login contract.
* Rotating to the current password is rejected (400) so the policy is
  meaningfully re-applied and the change is auditable as a real event.
* On success ``token_generation`` is bumped to revoke every
  outstanding access + refresh token — a password change must not
  leave old sessions live (this is the revocation point the
  ``/users/refresh`` reuse-detect comment already anticipates).

schema.title: Response Change My Password Api V1 Users Me Password Post

post.description:
Log out the authenticated user by revoking all outstanding tokens.

Bumps ``token_generation`` on the user row.  Every JWT access and
refresh token issued before this call embeds the previous
``gen`` value and will fail the equality check in
``get_current_user`` / ``/users/refresh`` on the next request.
The client must drop the local tokens; the server can't (and
shouldn't try to) revoke them out-of-band.

Idempotent: a second call from the same session is a no-op
against an already-revoked generation, just bumping the counter
further.  Returns 204 No Content.

schema.title: Response Verify Totp Setup Api V1 Users Totp Verify Post

post.description:
Invalidate every outstanding backup code and issue 10 fresh.

Requires password re-authentication, same as ``/totp/setup`` — a
stolen access token alone must NOT be able to swap in attacker-
controlled recovery codes.  LDAP / OIDC users hit a 400: there's
no password the server can verify, and gating the regenerate flow
on the upstream IdP would punt the security boundary out of our
control.

Returns the new codes ONCE in the response body.  The audit row
records the regenerate event with the new-code count but never any
of the cleartext codes (C3 invariant).

post.description:
Generate a new compliance evidence pack.

Admin-only: a pack is a permanent, monetized, audit-weight artefact —
the same trust level as the two-admin attestations it consumes.
Module-gated: returns 402 (and records the denial in the audit log) if
the active license does not entitle the requested framework.  Returns
404 for unknown frameworks, 503 when the signing key is unusable.

Idempotency: pass an ``Idempotency-Key`` header to make retries safe —
generation is a slow, request-path operation that can outlive a proxy
timeout after committing, so a naive client retry would otherwise mint a
second near-identical signed pack. A repeat with the same key returns the
already-generated pack instead.

Retry-safety is deliberately CLIENT-OWNED (the header), not a server-side
time-window dedup: only the client knows whether a second request is a
RETRY of the first or an intentional fresh generation of evolving fleet
state. A server-side "collapse identical requests within N seconds" rule
would wrongly merge two legitimate back-to-back generations (e.g. before and
after a remediation) into one pack. The dashboard therefore sends a fresh
UUID key per user-initiated generate; an un-keyed retry may mint a duplicate,
which is still an individually-valid signed pack (dedupable by
``content_sha256``).

get.description:
List evidence pack metadata, newest first, as ``{total, items}``.

Fail-closed listing: only packs of entitled frameworks are returned; an
explicit ``framework`` filter must name a KNOWN framework (404 otherwise,
matching the generate route) and an unentitled one is a 402.  Selects
metadata columns only — the JSONB ``frozen_inputs``/``payload`` blobs are
never loaded for a listing.

Re-derive the pack from frozen inputs and verify every integrity layer.

Verify is a diagnostic endpoint — a failing result is still returned
normally to the caller — but detections must be durable:

- **tampered** (payload/inputs/signature integrity broken) raises a
  critical Alert + audit event (see ``_record_reproduction_failure``).
- **collector drift** (intact artefact, changed collector code) is
  recorded as a non-critical audit event — a routine-upgrade signal,
  never a tamper alarm.
- a missing/corrupt signing key is 503 (verification cannot complete),
  not a tamper verdict — but a hash-layer tamper detection is recorded
  FIRST (payload/frozen-inputs verdicts do not depend on the key).

Render and stream a pack in the requested format (json|pdf|zip).

Downloads live under an explicit ``/download/{fmt}`` subpath with a
constrained ``DownloadFormat`` enum — deliberately NOT a greedy
``/{fmt}`` segment — so ``/verify`` and any future pack subresource can
never be shadowed by (or collide with) the format capture.

Every download re-verifies what it serves: the stored payload must match
its signed ``content_sha256`` AND the Ed25519 envelope must verify as
``True`` — otherwise nothing is served.  A hash failure is 500 plus a
durable critical Alert; an unverifiable signature (pack ``key_id`` not
the configured signing key — rotation/restore or a rewritten column) is
a 409 with operator guidance, because serving (or re-signing a ZIP of)
bytes whose signature cannot be checked would let a consistent DB
rewrite masquerade as verified evidence.  This cheap check (stored
payload hash + signature; no collector run, no frozen-inputs load)
guards the serving path; the full frozen-input reproduction diagnostic
lives on ``GET /packs/{id}/verify``.

get.description:
Conventional ``/health`` probe target.

Mirrors ``/api/live`` (cheap liveness check; no DB/Redis touch) and is
the canonical bypass entry in the license hard-fail middleware.  Both
Kubernetes-friendly probes and external uptime monitors expect this
path; the ``/api`` variants stay for back-compat.

Liveness probe target — returns 200 as long as the FastAPI
process is up and responsive.  Does **not** touch the database
or Redis: a slow or failed dependency shouldn't cause K8s to
kill and restart the pod (that just amplifies the outage).

Readiness (route-traffic-to-this-pod) is a separate concern —
see ``/api/ready``.

schema.title: Response Liveness Check Api Live Get

get.description:
Readiness probe target — returns 200 only when the pod is
actually able to serve requests: startup has completed, the DB
and Redis are reachable, and shutdown has not begun.  (CA
initialisation runs at startup; failures there are logged but
are not part of the readiness gate.)

On SIGTERM we flip ``_ready`` to False before uvicorn drains
in-flight requests, so the Service endpoints list removes this
pod before it stops accepting new connections.  Without that,
clients hit a 5xx window equal to the readiness-probe interval.

Back-compat deep-health endpoint.

Predates the ``/api/live`` + ``/api/ready`` split.  New
deployments should point livenessProbe at ``/api/live`` and
readinessProbe at ``/api/ready``; this endpoint keeps the old
behaviour (DB + Redis check, 503 if either unreachable) so
proxies / monitors that still hit ``/api/health`` continue to
work identically.

TrustedRegistryAuthIn.title: TrustedRegistryAuthIn
TrustedRegistryAuthIn.description:
Write-only credential payload accepted by PUT.

The fields are conditional on ``mode``:
  * ``none``   -> all credential fields ignored (and any existing
                   sibling row deleted on save).
  * ``bearer`` -> ``token`` required, ``username``/``password`` ignored.
  * ``basic``  -> ``username`` + ``password`` required, ``token`` ignored.

Validation lives in ``_normalise_auth`` below so PUT can produce
a uniform 422 message rather than a Pydantic schema error per
missing field per mode.

TrustedRegistryAuthOut.title: TrustedRegistryAuthOut
TrustedRegistryAuthOut.description:
Read-only auth state surfaced on GET.

The credential values are NEVER serialised here — the API contract
is 'is auth configured at all + what mode' so the dashboard can
render a ``••• configured (bearer)`` placeholder.  Operators who
need to inspect or rotate the actual secret do that by PUT'ing a
fresh value.

``rotated_at`` carries the UTC ISO-8601 timestamp at which the
*current* encrypted sibling row was written.  Each PUT that
changes a credential mints a fresh sibling row (new UUID); the
old row is GC'd by the same handler.  So this timestamp is
effectively "when the current credential value was last set" —
used by the dashboard to surface a 'Configured N days ago'
indicator with a warning when rotation is overdue.  ``None``
when ``configured`` is False, or when the sibling row has been
deleted out-of-band (orphan-GC bug + a stale public row).

TrustedRegistryRead.title: TrustedRegistryRead
TrustedRegistryRead.description:

auth field is the redacted ``TrustedRegistryAuthOut`` rather than
the write-only ``TrustedRegistryAuthIn``.  Separate types so an
accidental return of the write model can't leak a credential.
